title: California Lettuce Farmers Destroy Crops as Cyclospora Panic Tanks Demand
excerpt: Salinas Valley growers plow hundreds of thousands of pounds of healthy romaine back into the soil after a parasitic outbreak linked to Mexican imports crushes consumer confidence in fresh greens.
body:
• California growers are plowing healthy lettuce back into the ground as consumer demand plunges amid a cyclospora outbreak that has sickened nearly 2,000 people in nine states.
  • One Salinas Valley farmer dumped 300,000 pounds of romaine hearts this week despite no evidence linking domestic crops to the parasite.
  • Fresh lettuce sales fell 8.7% in July — more than 7.6 million pounds — while foot traffic at salad-heavy chains like Taco Bell dropped up to 21%.
  • Food safety experts warn the demand slump could persist for years, mirroring the fallout from the 2006 E. coli spinach crisis.

In the fertile fields of California’s Salinas Valley, Larry Cox is watching perfectly good lettuce rot. This week, the owner of Coastline Family Farms chopped 300,000 pounds of romaine hearts and plowed them back into the soil — not because the crop was contaminated, but because no one wants to buy it.

A Parasite Thousands of Miles Away

The culprit is cyclospora, an intestinal parasite that causes severe watery diarrhea, cramping, and fatigue. The current outbreak has sickened at least 1,947 people across nine states and been traced to iceberg lettuce from a Taylor Farms facility in central Mexico. But the fallout has spread far beyond that single supply chain, engulfing the entire American lettuce industry.

"It is incredibly demoralizing. I would’ve been better off taking a vacation in the South of France than planting the crop."

— Larry Cox, Coastline Family Farms

Salinas Valley, known as “America’s Salad Bowl,” produces nearly half of the nation’s lettuce. Cox supplies some of the country’s largest restaurant chains and grocery stores, yet his sales have plunged 20% to 30%. Many neighboring growers face the same predicament and are destroying crops they cannot sell.

Consumer Retreat Hits Hard

Data from NielsenIQ shows that unit sales of fresh lettuce slipped 8.7% through much of July compared with the prior year — a shortfall of more than 7.6 million pounds. Other fresh produce categories also saw declines as shoppers abandoned supermarket produce aisles entirely.

Restaurant chains built around salads have been hit especially hard. Foot traffic at salad-heavy outlets such as Taco Bell and Chopt has fallen as much as 21% year-to-date, according to the Wall Street Journal. Taco Bell has responded by rolling out steep discounts on lettuce-free menu items.

“Consumers aren’t sure what’s right anymore so, out of an abundance of caution, they’re just passing on everything,” said Joelle Mosso, who leads science and food safety programming at Western Growers, a family farm trade group.

Echoes of the Spinach Crisis

Max Teplitski, chief science officer for the International Fresh Produce Association, warned that major food-safety scares can suppress demand for years. The comparison he draws is to the 2006 E. coli outbreak linked to California spinach, which devastated the leafy-greens sector for an extended period.

For farmworkers in Salinas Valley, the consequences are immediate. Cox has already cut jobs, and with lettuce operating on a roughly 30-day growing cycle, farmers who plow under current crops must now decide whether to replant at all.

What Comes Next

Despite the gloom, Cox remains resolute. “You can’t afford to be downcast very long,” he said. “You better pick yourself up, dust yourself off and keep pushing forward.” Whether consumers regain confidence in domestic lettuce before the next planting cycle, however, remains an open question — one that could reshape California’s produce economy for seasons to come.
